questions.text: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?
questions.solution:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Sorted
Heap
Unclustered tree index
Unclustered hash index

questions.text: Which of the following statements about the Two Phase Locking (2PL) protocol is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- 2PL guarantees conflict serializability, so it permits only serializable schedules [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Locking just before each operation and releasing just after violates 2PL (a release followed by a new lock) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- Growing phase then shrinking phase: once a lock is released, no new lock can be acquired [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- Deadlock is possible: T1 locks A, T2 locks B, then each waits for the other [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Options 1, 3 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: 2PL permits only serializable schedules
With 2PL, a transaction always locks the data item being read or written just before every operation and always releases the lock just after the operation
With 2PL, once a lock is released on any data item inside a transaction, no more locks on any data item can be obtained inside that transaction
A deadlock is possible with 2PL

questions.text: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation is/are TRUE?
questions.solution:
Recall the IPv4 fragmentation rules:
- In IPv4, any router whose outgoing link MTU is smaller than the datagram can fragment it (not only the source).
- Fragments may take different routes, so reassembly is done only at the destination.

Answer: Options 2 and 3

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed only at the source of the datagram
The fragmentation of an IP datagram is performed at any IP router which finds that the size of the datagram to be transmitted exceeds the MTU
The reassembly of fragments is performed only at the destination of the datagram
The reassembly of fragments is performed at all intermediate routers along the path from the source to the destination

questions.text: Which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- An attribute grammar is an SDD whose semantic rules have no side effects [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (definition).
- "L-attributed definitions cannot always be evaluated in depth-first order" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. Every L-attributed definition can be evaluated by a left-to-right depth-first traversal; that is why they are called L-attributed.
- Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser during reductions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "All L-attributed definitions based on LR(1) grammars can be evaluated bottom-up" [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE. The marker non-terminal method is guaranteed only for L-attributed definitions on LL(1) grammars; adding markers can make an LR(1) grammar non-LR.

Answer: Options 2 and 4

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: An attribute grammar is a syntax-directed definition (SDD) in which the functions in the semantic rules have no side effects
The attributes in a L-attributed definition cannot always be evaluated in a depth- first order
Synthesized attributes can be evaluated by a bottom-up parser as the input is parsed
All  L-attributed  definitions  based  on  LR(1)  grammar  can  be  evaluated  using  a bottom-up parsing strategy

questions.text: For a Boolean variable [latex]x[/latex], which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]x\cdot1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (identity).
- [latex]x+1=x[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x+1=1[/latex].
- [latex]x\cdot x=0[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE, since [latex]x\cdot x=x[/latex] (idempotence).
- [latex]x+\bar{x}=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE (complement).

Answer: [latex]x+1=x[/latex] and [latex]x.x=0[/latex]
